tldr: The authors developed a toolchain that automatically builds accurate collision meshes and photo-realistic 3D Gaussian Splatting environments from casual smartphone videos. Using this, they built "Neverwhere," an evaluation benchmark of over 60 real-world environments for visual parkour with quadruped robots. They validated that simulation behaviors closely match real-world robot trials, while also uncovering the overfitting risks and limitations of training policies solely inside 3DGS environments.
hero_caption: Overview of the Neverwhere benchmark suite. It reproduces over 60 urban indoor and outdoor scenes using high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision meshes, enabling automated continuous testing via closed-loop simulation.
overview:
In recent years, visual locomotion controllers (visuomotor policies) for quadruped robots have made tremendous progress. However, there has been a lack of scalable, safe ways to evaluate their performance in complex real-world environments—such as outdoor curbs and stairs—prior to physical deployment. Traditional mesh-based manual simulators cannot fully reproduce realistic cluttered textures and geometries, while physical testing remains prohibitively expensive and risky.

To address this challenge, the authors developed "Neverwhere," blending 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), a modern 3D scene representation, with the physics simulator MuJoCo. They designed a semi-automated toolchain to generate accurate collision meshes and high-fidelity appearance models directly from uncalibrated videos captured on handheld cameras. With this toolchain, they curated over 60 diverse parkour scenes gathered across university campuses.

Running side-by-side evaluations on a real Unitree Go1 robot showed that success and failure patterns in simulation correlate strongly with real-world robot behavior (Sim-to-Real consistency). Furthermore, examining closed-loop imitation learning (DAgger/ACT) within this suite revealed single-scene overfitting and substantial generalization gaps across tasks, demonstrating that the environment is exceptionally valuable as an objective evaluation benchmark rather than merely a training ground.
contributions: Built an open-source pipeline to jointly reconstruct accurate collision meshes and 3DGS visual appearances from uncalibrated image collections.
Provided an evaluation benchmark suite for quadruped visual parkour comprising over 60 real-world scenes, including indoor and outdoor stairs, gaps, ramps, and hurdles.
Implemented a system coupling MuJoCo with 3DGS to deliver multimodal observations—such as RGB, depth, and point clouds—in real-time closed-loop simulation.

Demonstrated Sim-to-Real consistency through side-by-side comparisons between real-world trials and simulated twin scenes, and quantitatively uncovered the challenges of overfitting and generalization in 3DGS closed-loop training.

sections.heading: A Realistic Proving Ground for Robots Entering the Open World
sections.summary: While data-driven approaches have greatly improved visuomotor policies, relying only on real-world evaluations or manually crafted simulations limits scalable verification. This paper introduces "Neverwhere," a benchmark suite of over 60 environments capturing real-world complexity via 3DGS, along with its construction toolchain.
sections.details:
Evaluating robotics tasks where perception and action are tightly coupled—especially visual locomotion for legged robots—is notoriously difficult. Real-world visual complexity cannot be captured by conventional CAD meshes alone, yet testing every iteration directly on physical hardware is impractical.

To tackle this, the authors propose "Neverwhere," a benchmark comprising over 60 photo-realistic real-world scenes. It spans diverse urban structures, including stairs, speed bumps, carpeted laboratories, and outdoor areas with vegetation.

Building robot simulation environments from real-world scenes poses three major challenges:
- Real-world visual clutter cannot be fully represented by standard 3D meshes alone.
- A quadruped robot's low viewpoint differs drastically from handheld human cameras, making 3DGS prone to overfitting and rendering artifacts from out-of-distribution angles.
- Recovering an accurate collision mesh directly from handheld video is difficult.

To overcome these issues, the authors integrated classical Multi-View Stereo (MVS) geometry into both the initialization and regularization of 3DGS, establishing a pipeline that achieves both faithful collision geometry and robust novel-view synthesis.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from CAD Environments and Generative AI?
sections.summary: While physics engines like IsaacSim and ManiSkill3 continue to evolve, asset scarcity remains a bottleneck. Unlike manual CAD modeling or diversity-focused generative models, Neverwhere targets photo-realism paired with reliable collision geometry using 3DGS, delivering deterministic, noise-free evaluation standards.
sections.details:
Two main paradigms have dominated environment generation for robot learning.

First is manually creating high-quality CAD assets. For instance, BiGym offers articulated dishwasher meshes, and RoboCasa provides 14 human-designed kitchens. However, these require immense modeling labor and struggle to encompass open-world visual disorder.

Second is leveraging generative AI (video generation models and diffusion models) to enhance training data diversity. Examples include Cosmos and Veo. While effective for introducing variety during training, their high entropy makes them ill-suited for reproducible benchmark testing.

Neverwhere takes a distinctly different path. By adopting 3D Gaussian Splatting as a neural scene representation, it dramatically slashes asset creation costs while obtaining accurate collision geometry via MVS without LiDAR or depth sensors. Guided by the principle that evaluation benchmarks demand deterministic, reliable challenges over random diversity, it prioritizes a high signal-over-noise ratio during testing.

sections.heading: From Video to Physical Twins: A Geometry-Guided 3DGS Toolchain
sections.summary: The authors introduce a pipeline to automatically construct physically interactive digital twins from handheld video. Incorporating depth and mesh cues from MVS into 3DGS initialization and geometric regularization enables artifact-free rendering from low robot viewpoints alongside precise collision handling.
sections.details:
The processing workflow that converts an uncalibrated image collection $\mathcal{I}=\{\mathbf{I}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ into an interactive MuJoCo physical environment operates as follows:

### Pipeline Formulation and Components
First, a camera pose estimation module $\Theta$ (COLMAP) estimates camera poses $\mathcal{P}$. Next, a mesh reconstruction module $\Phi$ (OpenMVS) reconstructs a geometric mesh $\mathcal{M}$. Finally, a 3DGS module $\Psi$ optimizes the scene appearance.
Standard 3DGS tends to overfit training camera viewpoints, causing severe visual artifacts when rendered from the low eye-level of a quadruped. To resolve this, the method extracts depth maps $\mathbf{D}$ and confidence maps $\mathbf{C}$ produced during OpenMVS patch matching and incorporates them into 3DGS optimization as a geometric regularization loss. This allows geometrically consistent Gaussians to be optimized without any external depth sensors.

### Geometry-Guided Initialization and Mesh Fidelity
Gaussian initialization is also carefully designed. Rather than starting from sparse SfM points, the system samples point clouds directly from the textured mesh $\mathcal{M}$ reconstructed by OpenMVS. This places Gaussians neatly along real physical surfaces.
Furthermore, while meshes generated by consumer smartphone apps (like Polycam) often suffer from rounded edges that snag robot feet, the OpenMVS-based meshes maintain razor-sharp corners, delivering the geometric fidelity needed for delicate contact physics.

### Coordinate Alignment and Asset Evaluation
To align scale and ensure the Z-axis aligns with gravity, the authors built a web-based UI tool. With less than two minutes of human intervention—adjusting rotation and entering the measured real-world distance between two points—the model is metric-scaled and task waypoints are embedded. Quantitative evaluations across seven scenes using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS confirmed that adding geometric guidance consistently improves novel-view visual quality.

captions.F2: Overall workflow of the Neverwhere toolchain: (1) capturing video, (2) camera estimation via SfM, (3) geometric mesh reconstruction via MVS, (4) point sampling from the mesh, (5) training 3DGS with geometric regularization, (6) scale and pose alignment, and (7) waypoint placement in a streamlined flow.
captions.F5: Geometric improvements of the proposed approach. Compared to sparse SfM points (left), the proposed method (middle) reconstructs denser structure. Against rounded smartphone app meshes (Polycam), the proposed mesh (right) precisely captures sharp obstacle edges.

sections.heading: Four Parkour Tasks and a Multimodal Rendering Wrapper
sections.summary: Neverwhere introduces four parkour tasks for quadrupeds—hurdles, gaps, ramps, and stairs—quantifying success by the fraction of reached waypoints. It also includes an efficient rendering wrapper providing RGB, depth, point clouds, and semantics at high speeds.
sections.details:
Neverwhere contains over 60 scenes collected across two university campuses, running inside the MuJoCo physics engine. It targets the Unitree Go1 quadruped, whose action space controls target joint positions across 12 degrees of freedom (hip roll, hip pitch, knee pitch for each leg).

### IV-A Evaluation Task Design
To assess the generalization of locomotion policies, four tasks of varying difficulty are defined:
- **Hurdles**: Jumping over fixed-height obstacles or stone benches.
- **Gaps**: Leaping across chasms between separated platforms.
- **Ramps**: Traversing staggered, inclined planks with stability.
- **Stairs**: Ascending real-world staircases with diverse surface materials and step dimensions.
Each scene contains a canonical reference path defined by yellow waypoints (cones). The benchmark reports the "Success Rate" as the percentage of waypoints successfully traversed.

### IV-B Wrappers Supporting Rich Observation Modalities
To support visual policy research, the authors implemented high-speed rendering wrappers. Beyond photo-realistic 3DGS RGB rendering, the wrapper provides inverse depth maps in MiDaS format converted from MuJoCo's Z-buffer, simulated LiDAR point clouds, heightmaps, and semantic masks. It can also synthesize target markers (visual cones) directly into the scene to serve as goal-reaching visual cues for the policy.

captions.F6: Examples of supported observation modalities. Simulators can output 3DGS RGB images, collision geometries, MiDaS-formatted depth maps, and projected LiDAR point clouds in real time based on policy requirements.

sections.heading: Can We Trust Simulation Benchmarks for Real-World Deployment?
sections.summary: Using an existing visual policy (LucidSim), parallel evaluations were conducted in real-world scenes and their 1:1 Neverwhere digital twins. Matching success rates on hurdles and consistent relative difficulty across stairs confirm that Neverwhere serves as a reliable proxy for physical testing.
sections.details:
A high success rate in simulation is meaningless if the policy fails on hardware. To verify Sim-to-Real consistency, the authors took a pre-trained LucidSim policy and conducted 10 parallel evaluation rollouts per scene across matching physical environments and 1:1 Neverwhere digital twins.

The findings were highly revealing:
- **Hurdles (flat ground and obstacles)**: The simulation and the real robot achieved virtually identical completion rates, showing that visual domain gap artifacts were minimal.
- **Stairs**: Neverwhere simulation exhibited slightly higher success rates than the physical robot. This discrepancy stems from real-world contact complexities that are simplified in simulation, such as micro-slips of the footpads and slight step surface deformations.

Despite slight gaps in absolute numbers, the simulation and the real world displayed an astonishing correlation in "action and failure patterns"—specifically which scenes caused falls and which geometric setups triggered failures. This proves Neverwhere functions effectively as a pre-deployment proxy to uncover policy vulnerabilities.

captions.F8: Parallel evaluation between the physical robot and simulation across hurdles and stairs. Running the exact same policy yields closely aligned trajectories and failure modes, highlighting the suite's value as a pre-deployment validation platform.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Train Policies Directly in 3DGS?
sections.summary: The authors investigated closed-loop training within Neverwhere using DAgger and ACT architectures guided by a privileged expert. Single-scene training led to immediate overfitting, and multi-scene training still showed substantial performance drops on unseen scenes, underscoring that 3DGS is better suited for evaluation than pure policy training.
sections.details:
While Neverwhere was designed primarily as an evaluation benchmark, the authors explored what happens when 3DGS environments are used directly for closed-loop training (via reinforcement or imitation learning).

### Training Setup
A privileged teacher policy was trained with access to ground-truth elevation scans (ScanDots). An Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) student policy (operating on RGB or depth inputs) was then trained via DAgger over 4 iterations of 1,000 trajectories each.

### Single-Scene Training and the Overfitting Trap
When trained on a single scene, the student policy achieved near-perfect performance in that environment, but its performance collapsed when transferred to an unseen scene of the same task. Generalization was limited to cases with very close visual appearances (e.g., between two similar outdoor scenes), demonstrating severe visual overfitting.

### Multi-Scene Training and Modality Comparisons
Scenes for each task were split into 70% for training and 30% for evaluation, combined with visual domain randomization. On the Gaps task, the performance gap between seen and unseen environments was modest (~10%). However, on the challenging Stairs task, performance dropped by roughly 50%—falling from ~95% on training scenes to ~40% on unseen evaluation scenes.
Furthermore, comparing RGB and depth inputs showed that depth policies were surprisingly harder to optimize in closed-loop settings, resulting in slower training curves. Lastly, rendering visual cones directly into the scene as goal indicators clarified where the policy should attend, dramatically boosting generalization performance.

captions.F9: Closed-loop training curves across multiple scenes. (A) On the Stairs task, a large generalization gap (~50%) appears between training environments (blue) and unseen test environments (dashed red). (B)–(D) On Gaps, incorporating visual cones (D) yields the best training efficiency and unseen scene performance.

sections.heading: Toward Future Foundations for Robot Evaluation
sections.summary: Neverwhere offers a scalable, high-fidelity real-world digital twin evaluation suite for visual robot control. While it currently requires about one minute of manual scene alignment, future automation could extend this framework beyond legged locomotion to fields like manipulation.
sections.details:
As robot policies grow more expressive, rigorous and reproducible evaluation has become a major bottleneck. Neverwhere addresses this by providing a reliable, standardized testing foundation.

While this study focused on legged locomotion, the pipeline—converting casual video into contact-ready physical twins providing multimodal visual observations—naturally extends to wheeled robots and robotic manipulation.

A current limitation is that scale and the gravity axis (Z-up) are not determined automatically, requiring brief manual interaction. The authors plan to pursue fully automated pipelines in future work by incorporating learned pose-alignment techniques.

sections.heading: Appendix: One-Minute Scene Alignment and Extra Ablations
sections.summary: This section outlines the web-based annotation UI built on Vuer, which completes scale calibration, gravity alignment, and task setup in roughly one minute. It also covers additional experiments on all-task mixed training and observation ablations.
sections.details:
### Detailed Annotation Workflow
Models generated from uncalibrated video have arbitrary scale and coordinate orientations. To import them into MuJoCo, the authors built an annotation UI using the 3D visualization platform "Vuer":
- Load the mesh and rotate it so the gravity axis points Z-up (~20 seconds).
- Click two points on the mesh and input the real-world distance between them for automatic metric scaling (~10 seconds).
- Automatically clip mesh bounding boxes without manual cropping.
- Place target waypoints (cones) along the intended robot path (~15 seconds).
- Click save to export a ready-to-run MuJoCo XML scene.
The entire process takes about one minute, making it simple to ingest new environments rapidly.

### Additional Experiments: Multi-Task Training and Observation Ablations
When training a single ACT policy across all tasks and scenes combined, the policy achieved ~85% success on the training set, but suffered an approximate 30% drop on evaluation scenes. This highlights that collecting dozens of scenes is insufficient to train a universally generalized visual policy; while dozens suffice for benchmark evaluation, learning requires far greater data diversity.
Finally, ablating directional headings (yaw to the next waypoint) resulted in only a mild performance drop when visual cones were rendered, confirming that visual markers provide strong guidance cues on their own.

takeaways: Integrating 3DGS into robotics simulators requires regularizing and initializing Gaussians with MVS geometry (depth maps and reconstructed meshes) to prevent rendering failures from low robot viewpoints while ensuring accurate collision boundaries.

Because failure patterns in simulation correlate strongly with real-world failure patterns, 1:1 3DGS digital twins serve as powerful, safe environments for destructive stress testing prior to deployment.

Closed-loop training in 3DGS suites with dozens of scenes suffers from visual overfitting; currently, these environments are far more valuable as deterministic, objective evaluation benchmarks than as standalone training domains.
limitations: While mostly automated, determining the gravity direction, metric scale, and waypoint paths still requires 1 to 2 minutes of manual UI operation per scene.

Subtle contact dynamics—such as micro-slipping of rubber feet and step edge compliance—are simplified in simulation, leading to slightly optimistic success rates on challenging tasks like stairs compared to real hardware.
The framework is designed exclusively for static scenes and cannot simulate dynamic obstacles, wind-blown foliage, or terrain deformation under robot footfalls.
